{{Short description|French mathematician (1893–1948)}}
{{Distinguish|André Bloch (composer)|Spencer Bloch|Felix Bloch}}
'''André Bloch''' (20 November 1893 – 11 October 1948) was a French [[mathematician]] who is best remembered for his fundamental contribution to [[complex analysis]].

Bloch killed three of his family members, for which he was [[involuntary commitment|institutionalized]] in a [[mental asylum]] for 31 years, during which all of his mathematical output was produced.<ref name="macTutor">{{MacTutor|id=Bloch|title=Andre Bloch|date=December 1996}}</ref>

==Early life==
André Bloch was born in 1893 to a [[Jewish]] family in [[Besançon]], [[France]]. He was the eldest son in his family, his younger brother is Georges Bloch and his youngest brother is Henry Bloch. According to one of his teachers, [[Georges Valiron]], both André Bloch and his younger brother Georges Bloch were in the same class in October 1910.  Valiron believed Georges to have the better talent, and due to lack of preparation, André finished last in the class.  André was spared from failing the class by convincing [[Ernest Vessiot]] to give him an oral exam. The exam convinced Vessiot of Andre's talent and both André and Georges entered the [[École Polytechnique]].<ref name="valiron">G. Valiron, Des Théorèmes de Bloch aux Théories d'Ahlfors, Bulletin des Sciences Mathematiques 73 (1949) 152–162.</ref><ref name="campbell">D. Campbell, Beauty and the beast: The strange case of André Bloch, The Mathematical Intelligencer 7 (1985) 36–38.</ref>

Both brothers served for a year in the military prior to [[World War I]].<ref name="cartanFerrand">{{citation|first1=Henri|last1= Cartan|authorlink1=Henri Cartan| first2= Jacqueline|last2= Ferrand|authorlink2= Jacqueline Ferrand | title= The Case of André Bloch| journal=[[The Mathematical Intelligencer]]|volume= 10|issue=1 |year=1988|pages=23–26|doi=10.1007/BF03023847|mr=0918660|s2cid= 120041219}}</ref>  Both André and Georges studied for only one year at the [[École Polytechnique]] before the outbreak of the war.<ref name="cartanFerrand" />

==World War I==
Upon the outbreak of [[World War I]] in 1914, André and Georges Bloch were drafted. André, as a second-lieutenant in the artillery, was assigned to the headquarters of [[Noël Édouard, vicomte de Curières de Castelnau|General de Castelnau]] in [[Nancy, France|Nancy]].<ref name="cartanFerrand" />

Both Bloch brothers were injured: André suffered a fall from an observation post, while Georges sustained a head wound which cost him an eye.<ref name="cartanFerrand" /> Georges was released from service and returned to the École Polytechnique on 7 October 1917.<ref name="campbell" /> André, however, was allowed to convalesce but not released from duty.

==Murder==
On 17 November 1917, while on convalescent leave from service in [[World War I]], Bloch killed his brother Georges and his aunt and uncle.<ref name="macTutor" /> Several conjectures about the motives for Bloch's crime exist among mathematicians.<ref name="cambellMore">See the article by Campbell for several anecdotal examples. [[Henri Cartan]] and [[Jacqueline Ferrand]] note that "certain of these conjectures are outrageously eccentric".  [[Steven G. Krantz]] ("Mathematical Apocrypha: Stories and Anecdotes of Mathematicians and the Mathematical", American Mathematical Society, 2002) also lists some conjectures.</ref> However, Cartan and Ferrand quote [[Henri Baruk]], who was the medical head of the asylum where Bloch was confined. Bloch told Baruk that the murders were a [[eugenics|eugenic]] act, in order to eliminate branches of his family affected by mental illness.<ref name="cartanFerrand" />

==Commitment and mathematical career==
After the murders, Bloch was committed to the [[Charenton (asylum)|asylum at Charenton]] in [[Saint-Maurice, Val-de-Marne|Saint Maurice]],<ref name="cartanFerrand" /> a suburb of [[Paris]]. Bloch continued his mathematical career while confined. All of his publications, including those relating to [[Bloch's constant]], were written while he was committed. Bloch corresponded with several
mathematicians, including [[Georges Valiron]], [[George Pólya]], [[Jacques Hadamard]] and others,<ref name="cartanFerrand" /> giving his return address as only "57 Grande rue, Saint-Maurice", never mentioning that this was in a psychiatric hospital. Several of his correspondents were thus unaware of his confinement.<ref name="cartanFerrand" />

During the [[German military administration in occupied France during World War II|German occupation of France]], Bloch (who was [[Jewish]]) wrote under [[pseudonym|aliases]], in order to avoid advertising his presence to [[Nazi]] occupiers. In particular, Bloch is known to have authored papers under the names of René Binaud and Marcel Segond during this time.<ref name="campbell" />

According to Pólya, Bloch had the habit of dating his letters with 1 April,<ref name="campbell" /> regardless of when they were written.

Bloch was transferred to the [[Sainte-Anne Hospital Center|Sainte-Anne Hospital]] in Paris on 21 August 1948 for an operation. He died from [[leukemia]] in Paris on 11 October 1948.<ref name="cartanFerrand" />

==Mathematical work==
Most important works of Bloch belong to [[complex analysis]].

His early contribution is known as [[Bloch's theorem (complex variables)|Bloch's theorem]]. This theorem asserts the existence of a certain absolute constant which is called the Bloch constant. The exact value of the Bloch constant is still unknown {{as of|2026|lc=on}}. Research originating from this theorem led to introduction of Bloch's functions which form the so-called [[Bloch space]]. (This usage should not be confused with [[Bloch's theorem|Bloch's functions]] of Swiss physicist [[Felix Bloch]].)

Bloch formulated two important philosophical principles which proved to be useful in research in complex analysis. The more famous of these two is the so-called [[Bloch's principle]].<ref>{{cite journal|first=André |last=Bloch|title=La conception actuelle de la theorie des fonctions entieres et meromorphes|journal=[[L'Enseignement Mathématique]] |year=1926|volume=25|pages=83–103}}</ref>
In Bloch's own words it is formulated (in Latin) as follows:
"Nihil est in infinito quod non prius fuerit in finito", translated as "There is nothing in the infinite that did not exist before in the finite". Guided by this principle, Bloch was able to discover several important facts which were later proved by other mathematicians, for example, the [[Ahlfors theory#Five-island theorem|five-island theorem]]. There is an intensive current research related to Bloch's principle.

Bloch's ideas stimulated much of the research on [[holomorphic curve]]s in the 20th century and remain central in this subfield. He stated a fundamental theorem on holomorphic curves in complex [[manifold]]s whose irregularity exceeds dimension.<ref>{{cite journal|first=André|last=Bloch|title=Sur les systemes de fonctions uniformes satisfaisant a l'equations d'une variete algebriques dont l'irregularite depasse la dimension|journal=Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées|year=1926|volume=5|pages=19–66}}</ref> (This can be considered as a deep and far-reaching generalization of [[Picard theorem|Picard's theorem]].) His proof of this theorem contained gaps (which he recognized), and later the theorem was known as "Bloch's conjecture". Bloch's conjecture, as stated, was proved by Takushiro Ochiai, Pit Man Wong, and simultaneously by [[Yujiro Kawamata]] in 1980,<ref>{{cite book|title=Geometric function theory in several complex variables|first1=Junjiro|last1=Noguchi|first2=Takushiro|last2=Ochiai|year=1990|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|place=Providence RI}}</ref> and the related research started a new area which is called holomorphic curves in [[Abelian variety|Abelian varieties]] (and semi-Abelian varieties).

Bloch was the first (jointly with [[George Pólya|Pólya]]) to consider the distribution of roots of random polynomials,<ref>{{cite journal|first1=André|last1=Bloch|first2=George|last2=Pólya|title=On the roots of certain algebraic equations|journal=[[Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society]]|year=1931|volume=33|pages=102–114|doi=10.1112/plms/s2-33.1.102}}</ref> which is another area of research which is intensively developing
since the middle of 20th century.
